text:
The migration passed every staging run against a 40 GB snapshot seeded with synthetic rows. In production it failed forty minutes in, because the real orders table held 1.2 billion rows and a decade of drift.

The ALTER TABLE added a NOT NULL column with a default. On PostgreSQL 10, that forces a rewrite of the entire heap. The rewrite queued behind long-running checkout transactions, then demanded an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, and every later write had to wait for it. Requests piled up behind the lock, and connection pool exhaustion alerts paged on-call within ninety seconds.

Engineers had assumed the default was metadata-only. That fast path arrived in PostgreSQL 11, not 10. The rollback runbook had never been rehearsed, and it cost another twenty minutes. Staging had hidden the problem by leaving out the real table's size and drift.

Teams now shadow-migrate against full-size clones, set lock_timeout to 5 seconds to limit how long DDL can wait, and backfill in batches before tightening constraints. Some call this discipline "expand, then squeeze."
